multiplication.text: Multiplication means adding equal groups. When we say three times four, we mean three groups with four in each group.
Look at the rows. Count them all: four, eight, twelve. Three rows of four make twelve. So three times four equals twelve.
Here is a trick. Three times four and four times three give the same answer. You can flip the numbers to make it easier.
For the harder facts, skip count. For seven times three, count by sevens: seven, fourteen, twenty-one.

division.text: Division is sharing fairly. Twelve cookies shared with three friends. How many does each friend get?
Let's deal them out fairly: one for you, one for you, one for you, and again, until they are all gone. Each of the three friends gets four cookies. So twelve divided by three equals four.
Division is the opposite of multiplication. Because three times four is twelve, twelve divided by three is four. Use your times tables backwards!

fractions.text: A fraction shows part of a whole. The bottom number tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into, and the top number tells how many of those pieces we have.
Watch this. Two fourths covers the same amount of space as one half. They look like different numbers, but they are the exact same amount. We call those equivalent fractions.
When the bottom numbers match, the fraction with more pieces on top is the bigger one. Three fifths is more than two fifths because three pieces is more than two pieces.

When the top numbers are the same, look at the size of the pieces. The fewer pieces a whole is cut into, the bigger each piece is. So one half is more than one third. This trick only works when the tops match!

When the tops and the bottoms are both different, the fewer pieces trick can fool you. Make the bottoms match first. Two fifths is the same as four tenths, and four tenths is less than seven tenths. So seven tenths is bigger.

placeValue.text: Every digit sits in a special place. From the right, we have ones, then tens, then hundreds, then thousands. The place a digit sits in tells you its value.
Here is the secret of place value. Ten ones bundle together to make one ten. Ten tens bundle together to make one hundred. So each place is worth ten times the place to its right.
Look at the number one thousand two hundred thirty-four. The two is sitting in the hundreds place, so it is not just two. It really means two hundred.
To round to the nearest ten, look at the ones digit. If it is five or more, round up to the next ten. If it is less than five, round down and keep the ten you already have.

measurement.text: Area is the amount of space inside a shape. You can count all the little squares that fit inside, or take a shortcut and multiply the length times the width. Four times three equals twelve!
Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape, like walking around the edge of a yard. Add up every side: four plus three plus four plus three equals fourteen.
On a clock, the short hand points to the hour. The long hand points to the minutes, and it counts by fives: five, ten, fifteen. The short hand is just past the eight, so it is eight fifteen!
When you count money, count the dollars first: one dollar. Then count the cents: twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five. Put them together, and you have one dollar and seventy-five cents!

geometry.text: Shapes get their names from their sides and their corners. A square is special because it has four sides that are all the same length, and it has four corners.
Count the sides to name a shape. Three sides make a triangle. Four sides make a quadrilateral. Five sides make a pentagon, and six sides make a hexagon!
A corner, where two sides meet, is called an angle. The square corner that you see in a square is a special angle that we call a right angle.
An angle smaller than a right angle is called acute. It is narrow, like the tip of a pizza slice. An angle bigger than a right angle is called obtuse. It opens up wide.
Lines that run side by side and never cross are called parallel, like train tracks. Lines that cross to make square corners are called perpendicular, like a plus sign.
Let us check what you remember about a square. Think about its straight edges and count them carefully.

dataGraph.text: To collect data, make one tally mark for each fruit sold. The fifth mark crosses the other four, making a bundle of five. Count the bundle as five, then six, seven, eight. Eight plums!
A bar graph shows amounts using bars. Each bar stands for one thing, and the taller a bar is, the bigger its number. A short bar means a small number.
To read a bar, find its top, then slide straight across to the numbers on the side. The apple bar lines up with five, so five apples were sold. The tallest bar shows the biggest number.
How many more plums were sold than apples? Draw a line across from the top of the apple bar. The plum bar reaches three spaces higher: six, seven, eight. Eight minus five equals three!

wordProblem.text: First, read the problem slowly: A box has six rows of four crayons. How many crayons are there in all? Then picture the story in your mind. See the box, and the crayons lined up inside it.
Next, find the question the problem is asking, and then choose the right operation. When the story has equal groups, like rows that are all the same size, that is a clue to multiply.

Now solve it. There are six rows, and each row has four crayons, so we multiply six times four. Count by fours: four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty, twenty-four! There are twenty-four crayons in all.

reading.text: Good readers look for the main idea: what the whole passage is mostly about. Read each sentence and ask, who or what is it about? Frogs. Frogs. Frogs! So this passage is mostly about frogs.
Think of the main idea as a tabletop. The details are the legs that hold it up. Frogs live near ponds. Frogs eat insects. Frogs can jump far. Each detail tells us more about frogs.
For a detail question, go back into the text and find the exact words. Don’t guess from memory! What do frogs eat? Find the clue word, eat, in the passage. There it is: they eat insects.

Sometimes the answer is not written down, so you use clues. The text says frogs can jump very far. What do you know about jumping far? It takes strong legs! Clues plus what you know make an inference.

writing.text: A complete sentence has two parts. The naming part tells who or what the sentence is about. The action part tells what they do. And every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a punctuation mark.
Here is an example. The dog ran fast. The naming part is the dog, because that is who the sentence is about, and the action part is ran fast, because that tells what the dog does.
If a part is missing, it is not a complete sentence. The big dog. What did it do? Ran fast. Who ran? Put the parts together: The big dog ran fast. Now it is complete!
Every sentence ends with an end mark. A period ends a telling sentence. A question mark ends an asking sentence. And an exclamation point shows a strong feeling, like wow!

science.text: Matter comes in three states: solid, liquid, and gas. A solid keeps its own shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of whatever cup you pour it into. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can.
Water is amazing because it can be all three states. When it is frozen, ice is a solid. When you pour it, water is a liquid. And when it boils away, steam is a gas.

Water moves in a cycle. The sun warms the lake, and water rises as vapor. That’s evaporation. Up high, the vapor cools into tiny drops that make clouds. That’s condensation. When the drops get heavy, they fall as rain. That’s precipitation!

Plants make their own food! Leaves catch sunlight, roots soak up water, and leaves take in a gas called carbon dioxide. Using the sun’s energy, the plant turns them into sugar, and gives off the oxygen we breathe. That’s photosynthesis!

kCounting.text: Let's count the apples. Touch each apple one time. One. Two. Three. Four.
The last number tells how many. We stopped at four. So there are four apples!
Your turn! Here come some fish. Count them with your finger.
This is the number three. Three is one, two, three. Let's find three!

kShapes.text: This is a triangle. It has three straight sides. And three pointy corners!
This is a square. It has four sides, all the same size. And four corners!
This is a circle. It goes round and round. No sides, and no corners!
Some shapes are flat, like a square on paper. Some shapes are solid, like a box. This solid shape is a cube!

kLetters.text: Letters have names! Here is the letter A. Here is B. And here is C.
Letters come big and little. This is big B. This is little b. They are both B!
Listen to how these words start. Ball. Bear. Bus. They all start with B!
Your turn! Listen to the start of each word. Does it start like ball?

kRhymes.text: Listen to the end of each word. Cat. Hat. Bat. They sound the same at the end. They rhyme!
Moon and spoon rhyme, too. Moon, spoon! Now you find a rhyme.
Words have parts. Let's clap them! Ti… ger. Tiger has two claps!
Your turn! Clap the parts of banana. Ba… na… na!

kTracing.text: Let's trace! Find the green dot. That is where we start.
Follow the arrow. Big line down. Then a little line across. That's L!
Now O. Start at the green dot. Go around like a C. Keep going, all the way around. That's O!
Your turn! Start at the dot, and follow the arrow. You can do it!

kAddTake.text: Three frogs sit on a log. Two more hop on! Now there are five frogs.
Five ducks swim in the pond. Then two swim away. Bye, ducks!
This is a ten frame. It has ten spots. Seven are full. Three more make ten!
Your turn! Six spots are full. Look at the empty spots.

kStoryMath.text: Listen to a story. Bear has two apples. Fox brings her three more!
Let's act it out. Put them together and count. One, two, three, four, five. Five apples!
Owl sees six birds in a tree. Then two birds fly away.
Your turn! Bunny has three pears and two peaches.

kCompare.text: Is there a cookie for every friend? Let's line them up. One, two, three.
One friend has no cookie. More friends, fewer cookies. Now one more cookie. They are the same!
Your turn! Here come bears and balls. Does every bear get a ball?
Numbers can be more, too. Four dots, seven dots. Seven is more!

kTeens.text: This is a ten-frame. It has ten boxes. When every box is full, that's a full ten!
A full ten, and three more. Ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen. Ten and three more is thirteen!
Your turn! Look at the full ten. Then count on.
Every teen number is ten and some more. Let's find twelve!

kMeasure.text: Look at the two snakes. Let's line them up at the start. Now look at the ends. This snake is longer!
Your turn! A snake and a caterpillar. They start at the same place.
Now two towers. One stands on a box. Stand them on the same ground. This tower is taller!
This is a scale. The heavy side goes down. The light side goes up!

kSorting.text: Sorting means putting things that go together. Animals go in this box. Food goes in that box!
Now count each group. Let's count the animals!
We can sort by color, too. Red ones go here. Blue ones go there!
Look at the two groups. Count each one. Which group has more?

kScience.text: Look at the sky! It can be sunny, rainy, snowy or windy.
Uh oh, rain! We want to stay dry. Your turn!
Plants need sun and water. Animals need food, water and a home.
A push moves it away. A pull brings it close. Your turn!

kTowers.text: Critters are coming down the path! Let's keep them away from the house.
Tap a spot. Answer the question. Pop! A tower!
Your turn! Count the critters with your finger.
Towers stop the critters. Tap a tower to make it stronger!

g1Reading.text: Listen to the middle of a word. Cat. Kuh… aa… tuh. The A in the middle says aa!
Some letters team up to make one sound. S and H say shh, like ship and shell!
Now read a word. Sound it out: shh… ih… puh. Put the sounds together. Ship!
When we read along, each word lights up. The cat is on the mat. Your turn!

g1Writing.text: Little letters live on the lines. Tall ones touch the top line. Small ones start at the dashed line.
Let's trace a little a. Around like a C. Then a little line down.
To spell a word, say it slowly. Cat. Kuh… aa… tuh. Three sounds, three letters!
A sentence starts with a capital letter. It ends with a period. The dog ran.

g1Tens.text: Here are ten little cubes. Snap them together, and they make one rod. One rod is a ten!
Three rods and six cubes. Ten, twenty, thirty. Thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four, thirty-five, thirty-six! Three tens and six ones make thirty-six.
Your turn! Count the tens first. Then count on the ones.
Forty-one or fourteen: which is bigger? Look at the tens first. Four tens beat one ten. Forty-one is bigger!
This sign means greater than. Its open side faces the bigger number. Your turn!

g1Shares.text: Two friends share one pizza. Is this fair? No! One share is too big. Fair shares are the same size. They are equal shares!
Two equal shares are called halves. Each share is one half. Your turn!
Now cut each half again. Four equal shares! They are called fourths, or quarters.
More shares make smaller shares. A fourth is smaller than a half. Your turn!

g1Shapes.text: A triangle has three straight sides and three corners. It is closed, with no gaps.
Make it big or small. Paint it blue. Turn it around. It is still a triangle! Your turn!
Shapes can make new shapes. Two triangles snap together. Now they make a square!
A sphere can roll. A cube can stack. A cylinder can roll and stack! Your turn!

g1Measure.text: Line them up at the start. Look at the ends. Longest first, then the next one, then the shortest!
Lay paper clips end to end. No gaps, and no overlaps. This pencil is five clips long. Your turn!
This is a clock. The short hand shows the hour. The long hand points up to twelve. It is three o'clock!
Now the long hand goes down to six. The short hand moves halfway to four. It is half past three! Your turn!

g1Graphs.text: Our friends picked their favorite fruit. Put each one in its row. One picture for each friend!
Now count each row. Four friends like apples. Your turn!
The longest row has the most. Apples! The shortest row has the fewest. Bananas!
How many more like apples than grapes? Match them up, one with one. One apple has no match. One more! Your turn!

g1Science.text: Tap a drum. Its top shakes very fast. Things that shake make sound!
We need light to see. Light goes through glass. Wood blocks the light and makes a shadow! Your turn!
In the day, we see the sun. At night, we see the moon and stars. The sun comes up, and goes down.
A puppy looks like its mom, but not just the same. Parents feed their babies and keep them warm. Your turn!

g1Adding.text: Eight plus three. Start at eight. Count on: nine, ten, eleven!
Your turn! Two plus nine. Turn it around: start at nine.
Eight plus five. Move two to make ten. Ten and three is thirteen!
Your turn! Six and six. That is a double.

g1Subtract.text: Nine take away three. Cross out three. Six are left!
Your turn! Twelve minus three. Hop back three.
Thirteen minus five. Think addition! Five plus eight makes thirteen. So the answer is eight.
Your turn! Three, five and eight are a family.

g1StoryMath.text: Bear has eight apples. Fox brings five more. Eight plus five is thirteen!
Your turn! Owl saw twelve birds. Some flew away. Now nine are left.
Bunny picks four tulips, six roses and three daisies. Four and six make ten. Ten and three is thirteen!
Your turn! Bear has nine pears. Fox has six pears.

g5Reading.text: A theme is the big lesson a story teaches. It is not just what happens. To find it, watch how the main character changes. Rafi’s bridge falls apart, he rebuilds it with triangles, and it holds. What did he learn? Mistakes can teach us how to do better. That is the theme.

Writers paint pictures with figurative language. A simile compares two things using like or as: the bridge sagged like a tired horse. A metaphor says one thing is another: the quilt is a map of her life. An idiom is a saying that means something different from its words: to spill the beans means to tell a secret.

Who is telling the story? If the narrator says I and we, the story is told in first person, by a character inside it. If the narrator says he, she and they, it is third person, told from outside. A first person narrator only knows their own thoughts, so their feelings color everything we read.

Nonfiction has a shape, called its structure. Signal words give it away. First, next, then and finally mean time order. Because and so mean cause and effect. Both, but and however mean compare and contrast. A problem, then a fix, means problem and solution.

Sometimes you read two texts about the same topic. Put them side by side. What do both texts say? Where do they differ? A sailor’s logbook shares feelings about a storm. A news report sticks to facts and quotes. Same event, two points of view.

g5Writing.text: A strong opinion piece is built like a sandwich. Start with your opinion. Then give a reason, and back it up with evidence: a fact or an example. Add another reason with its evidence. Finish by saying your opinion again in new words.

Linking words are bridges between ideas. Use because to give a reason. Use for example to show evidence. Use also and in addition to add more. Use however to turn to a different idea, and therefore to show a result.

Informative writing teaches a reader. Begin with a topic sentence that tells what you will explain. Group facts that belong together into a paragraph. Start a new paragraph for a new idea. End with a conclusion that wraps it all up.

Dialogue makes characters talk. Put the spoken words inside quotation marks. The comma or end mark goes inside the closing quotation mark, before the speaker tag. Start a new paragraph each time a new character speaks.

Good stories have pacing. Slow down at the exciting moment: describe what the character sees, hears and feels. Speed up the boring parts with transitions like later that day, meanwhile, and after that. Then give your story a real ending.

g5Science.text: All matter is made of particles too small to see. Stir 20 grams of salt into 200 grams of water. The salt seems to vanish, but its particles are still there. Put it on a scale: 220 grams. When matter mixes, melts or dissolves, the total weight stays the same.

Energy for almost every food web starts with the sun. Grass captures sunlight to make food. A rabbit eats the grass, and a fox eats the rabbit. When they die, decomposers like mushrooms break them down and return matter to the soil. Matter cycles around. Energy keeps coming from the sun.

Scientists see Earth as four spheres. The geosphere is rock and soil. The hydrosphere is water and ice. The atmosphere is the air. The biosphere is every living thing. They interact all the time: when tree roots crack a rock, the biosphere is changing the geosphere.

If all of Earth’s water filled 100 cups, 97 cups would be salty ocean water. Only 3 cups would be fresh, and most of that is frozen in glaciers and ice caps. That is why the fresh water we can use is so precious.

The sun is a star. It looks brighter than other stars because it is much closer. Each day Earth spins once, so the sun seems to cross the sky. In the morning the sun is in the east, and shadows point west. At noon shadows are shortest. In the evening they point east.

g5Fractions.text: To add one half and one third, the pieces have to be the same size. Halves and thirds don't match. Cut both into sixths! One half is three sixths, and one third is two sixths. Three sixths plus two sixths is five sixths.

With mixed numbers, add the whole numbers, then add the fractions. Two and one half plus one and one third is three, plus five sixths: three and five sixths. When you subtract and the first fraction is too small, trade one whole for more pieces.

Check your answer with benchmarks. Two fifths is a little less than one half. Add one half, and the sum must be a little less than one whole. An answer like three sevenths is too small, so it can't be right.

To multiply two thirds times three fourths, shade three fourths of a square one way, then two thirds of it the other way. The overlap is six of twelve equal pieces. Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms: six twelfths, which is one half.
Three fourths times eight means three fourths of eight. Split eight into four equal groups of two. Three of those groups make six.

A fraction is also a division. Three pizzas are shared by four friends. Cut each pizza into fourths. Every friend gets one fourth of each pizza, so three fourths in all. Three divided by four is three fourths.

g5Decimals.text: Decimal places keep going to the right of the ones: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. Each place is worth ten times the place to its right. In three point four seven two, the four is four tenths, the seven is seven hundredths, and the two is two thousandths.
Read three point four seven two as three and four hundred seventy-two thousandths. The word and stands for the decimal point, and the last digit's place names the fraction.

Compare decimals place by place from the left, not by how long they are. Which is bigger, zero point five or zero point four five? Five tenths beats four tenths, so zero point five is greater. Writing a zero helps: zero point five zero is more than zero point four five.
To round three point four seven six to the nearest tenth, look one place to the right, at the hundredths digit. It's a seven, which is five or more, so round up: three point five.

Multiplying by ten makes every digit worth ten times more, so the digits slide one place to the left. Three point four five times ten is thirty-four point five, and times one hundred is three hundred forty-five. Dividing by ten slides them to the right.

To add, line up the decimal points so tenths add to tenths: four point five plus two point three seven is six point eight seven. To multiply zero point six times zero point four, multiply six times four, which is twenty-four. Tenths times tenths make hundredths, so the answer is zero point two four.

g5Volume.text: Volume is the amount of space inside a solid. We measure it in cubes. Build the bottom layer: four cubes long and three cubes wide makes twelve cubes. Stack three layers, and the box holds thirty-six cubes. That is thirty-six cubic centimeters!

Here is a shortcut. Length times width tells you the cubes in one layer. Multiply by the height to count every layer. Volume equals length times width times height: four times three times three is thirty-six.
The bottom face is called the base. Its area, B, is the number of cubes in one layer. So volume also equals B times h. A base of twelve square centimeters and a height of three make thirty-six.
This figure is made of two boxes that do not overlap. Find the volume of each box, then add. Twenty-four plus twelve equals thirty-six cubic meters.
To change to a smaller unit, multiply: one meter is one hundred centimeters, so three meters is three hundred centimeters. To change to a bigger unit, divide: one hundred twenty minutes is two hours.

g5Coordinates.text: A coordinate plane is two number lines that meet at zero. The x-axis goes across. The y-axis goes up. They meet at the origin, the point zero, zero.
An ordered pair is a set of directions. Start at the origin. The first number tells how far to go across. The second number tells how far to go up. Three, five means across three, then up five.
Grids help solve real problems. On this map, the library is at one, two, and the park is at one, seven. They share an x-coordinate, so count straight up: the park is five blocks from the library.

Shapes belong to families. A quadrilateral has four sides. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. A square is both!
So every square is a rectangle, because it has four right angles. But not every rectangle is a square, because its sides do not have to be equal.

g5LinePlots.text: Scientists measured ten bean sprouts to the nearest eighth of an inch. A line plot puts an X above the number line for each measurement.
Count the Xs above a mark. Three sprouts were four eighths, or one half, of an inch tall. The tallest stack shows the most common height.
To find a total, add the measurements. The two sprouts at five eighths of an inch add up to ten eighths, which is one and one fourth inches.
Four beakers hold one fourth, one half, one half and three fourths of a liter. What if we shared the water equally? Add it all: two liters. Then divide by four beakers: each gets one half liter.

Two patterns can make ordered pairs. Pattern A adds three: zero, three, six, nine. Pattern B adds six: zero, six, twelve, eighteen. Pair them up and plot them. The points make a line, and each B number is twice its A number.

g5Multiplication.text: To multiply twenty-three by fourteen, split each number by place value. Twenty-three is twenty plus three, and fourteen is ten plus four. Draw a rectangle and cut it into four boxes, one for each pair of parts. This is an area model.
Now fill each box. Twenty times ten is two hundred. Twenty times four is eighty. Three times ten is thirty. Three times four is twelve. These four numbers are the partial products.
Add the partial products: two hundred, plus eighty, plus thirty, plus twelve, makes three hundred twenty-two. So twenty-three times fourteen is three hundred twenty-two.

The standard algorithm does the same work in two rows. First multiply by the ones: twenty-three times four is ninety-two. Then multiply by the tens: twenty-three times ten is two hundred thirty. Add the two rows to get three hundred twenty-two.
Multiplying by ten moves every digit one place to the left. Ten to the third power means ten times ten times ten, which is one thousand. So six times ten to the third power is six thousand.

g5Division.text: Long division splits a big number one place at a time. Let's divide six hundred seventy-two by twenty-eight. The twenty-eight goes outside the bar, and six hundred seventy-two goes inside.

Twenty-eight does not fit in six, so look at sixty-seven. Twenty-eight is close to thirty, and thirty fits in sixty-seven two times. Two times twenty-eight is fifty-six. Sixty-seven minus fifty-six leaves eleven.

Bring down the two to make one hundred twelve. Twenty-eight fits in one hundred twelve four times, because four times twenty-eight is one hundred twelve. Nothing is left, so six hundred seventy-two divided by twenty-eight is twenty-four.

Sometimes there is a remainder. One hundred fifty-seven students ride buses that hold twenty-four each: that is six remainder thirteen. Those thirteen students still need a seat, so we round up to seven buses. If a question asks only for full groups, we drop the remainder. If it asks what is left over, the remainder is the answer.

g5Expressions.text: Every expression has an order. Work inside the grouping symbols first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. In three plus four times five, multiply first: four times five is twenty, and three plus twenty is twenty-three.

Parentheses change the order. Put three plus four in parentheses, then times five. Now we add first: three plus four is seven, and seven times five is thirty-five. Brackets work the same way, around the parentheses.

Words can turn into an expression. Add eight and seven, then multiply by two. The adding happens first, so eight plus seven goes inside parentheses, and we write two times that group. Without working it out, we know it is twice as large as eight plus seven.

Two patterns can grow side by side. Pattern A starts at zero and adds three: zero, three, six, nine. Pattern B starts at zero and adds six: zero, six, twelve, eighteen. Each term in pattern B is twice the matching term in pattern A.

A multi-step problem hides two steps in one story. A class buys six packs of twenty-four markers and gives thirty away. First multiply: six times twenty-four is one hundred forty-four. Then subtract thirty: one hundred fourteen markers are left.
